Field surveys of Kanshirei Village frog (Rana sauteri) in its montane stream habitats of central Taiwan have yielded detailed morphometric data across the life cycle. Freshly deposited eggs, measuring approximately 3.6 mm in diameter, give rise to hatchlings with a remarkably low wet weight at birth of 0.0244 grams [Wwb = 0.0244 grams], a mass that is typical for small ranid frogs and reflects the limited yolk reserves available for embryonic development. The endotrophic tadpole stage, which relies entirely on internal yolk reserves, precedes the onset of filter feeding. Larval development proceeds through a series of Gosner stages, culminating in metamorphosis at a snout–vent length of 1.36 cm . This size at metamorphosis is relatively modest compared to other ranid frogs occupying similar cool, fast-flowing streams, likely reflecting the constraints imposed by the unpredictable food supply typical of these headwater environments. Following metamorphic climax, the froglets emerge onto the adjacent forest floor.

Under a constant 15 °C [T = 15 °C] regime, puberty occurs at 730 days after birth [tp = 730 days after birth], marking the onset of gonadal maturation in female Kanshirei Village frogs. At this developmental milestone, the average snout–vent length reaches 3.2 cm [Lp = 3.2 cm], a threshold that marks the onset of vitellogenesis and the ability to produce mature oocytes. The post-metamorphic growth period leading to this size is characterized by steady somatic development, with individuals gradually transitioning from a purely insectivorous diet to one that includes larger terrestrial arthropods. Field-based recapture studies generally corroborate these laboratory findings, although some variation in age at maturation has been noted across different elevational gradients, with populations at higher altitudes tending to mature slightly later.

Sexually mature female Rana sauteri reproduce at a maximum rate of 225 eggs per year [Ri = 225 eggs per year] when maintained at 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This reproductive output is relatively modest compared to explosive-breeding ranids but consistent with a prolonged, low-intensity breeding strategy typical of montane stream-dwelling frogs. Egg masses are deposited in gelatinous clutches attached to submerged vegetation or rocks in shallow, well-oxygenated riffles. Parental investment beyond oviposition is absent, with embryo and larval survival depending entirely on abiotic conditions and predation pressure within the stream environment.

Adult body size exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in this species, with females attaining substantially larger dimensions than males. The ultimate snout–vent length recorded for females reaches 5.8 cm [Li = 5.8 cm], whereas males achieve a maximum of only 4.6 cm [Li = 4.6 cm]. This disparity in size is accompanied by a corresponding difference in mass, with the ultimate wet weight for females reaching 14.4 grams [Wwi = 14.4 grams]. Such dimorphism is common among ranid frogs and is generally attributed to fecundity selection, where larger body size in females allows for the production of larger clutches or larger eggs. The growth trajectory toward these asymptotic sizes slows markedly after the onset of reproduction, as energy is increasingly diverted from somatic growth toward gamete production.

Longevity data for Rana sauteri, derived from mark-recapture studies and captive observations, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years] when individuals are maintained at a constant 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This lifespan is relatively long for a frog of its body size, particularly when compared with lowland ranids that often experience higher predation rates and more rapid metabolic senescence. The extended lifespan likely reflects the cooler, more thermally stable environment of the montane streams and surrounding cloud forest. Older individuals, particularly those beyond five years of age, show signs of reproductive senescence, including reduced clutch sizes and lower hatching success. The population's age structure is consequently skewed toward younger adults, with the majority of reproductive effort concentrated in the first two to three years of adult life.
